summary: Cholinesterase inhibitor used for mild, moderate, and severe Alzheimer’s dementia and some other dementias. Modest benefits on memory and daily function, with common GI side effects and risks of bradycardia and weight loss.
description: Donepezil is a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. It increases levels of acetylcholine in the brain to support memory, attention, and daily function in people with Alzheimer’s disease and some other dementias. Benefits are usually modest and do not stop underlying neurodegeneration, but can slow decline or improve function for some patients. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, and weight loss. It can also slow the heart rate and occasionally provoke arrhythmias or syncope, so cardiac risk needs to be considered, especially in older adults with conduction disease or on other cardioactive medications.
patient_summary: Donepezil (Aricept, Adlarity patch) is a memory medicine for Alzheimer’s and related dementias. It doesn’t cure dementia, but it can help some people think more clearly, stay more independent with daily tasks, or slow decline for a period of time. Upsides can include better attention, remembering appointments, or being more engaged in conversation. Downsides often include nausea, diarrhea, poor appetite, weight loss, and trouble sleeping. It can also slow the heart and occasionally cause fainting. The decision to start or continue donepezil is very individual and should be revisited over time with the patient and caregivers.

primary.context: Approved for mild, moderate, and severe Alzheimer’s dementia to improve or stabilize cognition and daily function.

off_label.context: Used off-label in Parkinson disease dementia to support attention, memory, and visual hallucinations.
Often used off-label to improve hallucinations, fluctuations, and cognitive symptoms.
Sometimes used when vascular and Alzheimer pathology coexist; benefits tend to be modest.

therapeutic_response.display: Cognitive and functional benefits are typically evaluated over weeks to months; pharmacologic steady state is reached in about 2–3 weeks (oral) and slightly longer with patch.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: Up to ~15–20%, especially during first 4–6 weeks or dose increases
common_adverse_effects.notes: Usually improves within 1–3 weeks. Taking with food and slower titration can help. Persistent vomiting or diarrhea needs attention, especially in frail patients.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: A few percent overall; higher in low-weight patients and at higher doses (≥10 mg/day, especially 23 mg)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Regular weight checks are important. Worsening frailty or weight loss may prompt dose reduction, switch, or discontinuation.
Taking the dose earlier in the evening instead of at bedtime sometimes reduces sleep disruption and vivid dreams.
May relate to bradycardia or hypotension. Any fainting spells should trigger cardiac evaluation and fall-risk assessment.
Cramps are usually mild but can be bothersome; very severe pain or dark urine may suggest rare rhabdomyolysis and requires urgent evaluation.

serious_risks.risk: Bradycardia, AV block, or other arrhythmias (including QT prolongation and torsades de pointes)
Syncope leading to falls and injury
GI bleeding or perforated peptic ulcer
Rhabdomyolysis with muscle pain, weakness, and kidney injury
Severe contact dermatitis or widespread rash with patch use
Clinically significant weight loss and frailty in older adults

contraindications.contraindication: Known hypersensitivity to donepezil, piperidine derivatives, or any component of the formulation
History of serious contact dermatitis from donepezil transdermal patch (for patch use)
Canadian labeling: history of QT prolongation or torsades de pointes, including congenital long QT syndromes (relative/absolute depending on local guidance)
Canadian labeling: significant cardiac arrhythmias (eg, clinically important conduction disease)

precautions: Cardiac conduction risks: Donepezil can cause bradycardia, heart block, QT prolongation, and rarely torsades de pointes. Syncope and falls may occur.
GI effects and weight loss: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite, and weight loss are common; frail or low-weight patients are at higher risk.
Rhabdomyolysis: Rare cases of muscle breakdown with elevated CK, muscle pain, dark urine, and kidney injury have been reported.
Peptic ulcer and GI bleeding: Increased gastric acid secretion may worsen ulcers or trigger GI bleeding, especially with NSAIDs or anticoagulants.
Respiratory disease: Can increase bronchoconstriction; use caution in asthma or COPD.
Seizure risk: Cholinergic stimulation may lower seizure threshold in susceptible patients, although seizures can also be due to underlying dementia.
Urinary obstruction: Can increase bladder outflow resistance and worsen symptoms in patients with urinary tract obstruction.
Patch-specific reactions: Adlarity patches can cause local skin reactions and, rarely, contact dermatitis.

interactions.interactant: Beta-blockers, digoxin, some calcium channel blockers
interactions.mechanism: Additive bradycardia and conduction delay; higher risk of syncope and falls.
interactions.action: Monitor pulse and blood pressure; consider ECG in high-risk patients; adjust doses or reconsider therapy if significant bradycardia occurs.

interactions.interactant: Other drugs that prolong QT (eg, certain antipsychotics, macrolides, class III antiarrhythmics)
interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, especially in patients with other risk factors.
interactions.action: Avoid combinations in patients with strong QT-risk profiles when possible; monitor ECG if combined.

interactions.mechanism: Increased risk of GI bleeding because donepezil boosts gastric acid and may impair mucosal defense.
interactions.action: Use GI protection strategies in high-risk patients; monitor for bleeding signs (black stools, vomiting blood, anemia).

interactions.interactant: Anticholinergic medications (eg, oxybutynin, benztropine, diphenhydramine, some tricyclics)
interactions.mechanism: Mechanistic opposition—anticholinergics may blunt or negate donepezil’s benefits.
interactions.action: Minimize chronic anticholinergic use in dementia; consider alternative agents with lower anticholinergic burden.

interactions.interactant: Strong CYP3A4 or CYP2D6 inhibitors or inducers
interactions.mechanism: May alter donepezil plasma concentrations; clinical impact is usually modest but can contribute to side effects or reduced efficacy.
interactions.action: Monitor for increased side effects or loss of effect when starting or stopping strong inhibitors/inducers; adjust clinical plan based on response.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Cognition and function: Regular assessments of memory, orientation, language, daily functioning, and caregiver burden (eg, every 6–12 months).
Behavioral symptoms: Track hallucinations, agitation, sleep changes, and mood; adjust therapy and non-drug strategies accordingly.
Heart rate and blood pressure: Especially in the first months and after dose changes; consider ECG in patients with known conduction disease or on QT-prolonging agents.
Weight and nutritional status: Baseline and periodic weights to detect clinically significant weight loss or frailty.
GI tolerance: Ask about nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and appetite, particularly during titration.
Signs of GI bleeding: Monitor for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, or unexplained anemia in at-risk patients.
Patch site (if transdermal): Inspect for significant erythema, edema, blistering, or signs of contact dermatitis.
Falls and syncope: Ask about new falls or near-syncope; evaluate for bradycardia, hypotension, or arrhythmias.

special_populations.pregnancy: Donepezil is rarely used in pregnancy, since dementia syndromes are uncommon in reproductive-age individuals. Animal data show some adverse fetal effects, but human data are limited. If a pregnant patient on donepezil requires ongoing treatment, the potential benefits should clearly outweigh risks, and non-pharmacologic support for cognition should be optimized.
special_populations.lactation: It is unknown whether donepezil passes into human breast milk. Use in breastfeeding is rarely relevant clinically given the typical age of patients. If needed, risks to the infant, potential benefits to the parent, and alternative treatments should be considered.
special_populations.pediatric: Donepezil is not a standard treatment for children or adolescents; pediatric use would be highly specialized and off-label (eg, rare neurodegenerative conditions) and requires subspecialty oversight.
special_populations.geriatric: Most treated patients are ≥65 years. Age-related decreased clearance means higher exposure at a given dose. Frailty, low body weight, conduction disease, and polypharmacy (especially cardioactive and QT-prolonging drugs) raise risk. Start low, titrate slowly, and reassess benefit vs. burden regularly.
special_populations.renal_impairment: Donepezil is highly protein-bound and not significantly dialyzed. No routine dose adjustment is needed in kidney impairment, including hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, but monitoring for tolerability remains important.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: In stable alcoholic cirrhosis, donepezil clearance decreases by about 20%. No formal dosing adjustment is specified, but caution and slower titration are recommended in hepatic impairment.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral: well absorbed; transdermal: slower uptake with gradual attainment of steady-state.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: High oral bioavailability; food has minimal effect on overall exposure.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Oral tablet 10 mg: ~3 hours; 23 mg: ~8 hours; transdermal: ~7 days to peak.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Oral: ~70 hours; transdermal: ~91 hours; supports once-daily oral dosing and once-weekly patch dosing.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism via CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 and glucuronidation to multiple metabolites, two of which are active.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: About 57% in urine (∼17% unchanged), ~15% in feces.
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: ~96% protein-bound, mainly to albumin and alpha1-acid glycoprotein.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food may delay but does not meaningfully alter the extent of oral absorption.

dosing.titration: Dosing is typically once daily for oral formulations and once weekly for the patch, with slow titration to minimize GI and cardiac side effects.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Donepezil is not physically addictive, but abrupt discontinuation can lead to noticeable cognitive or behavioral worsening in some patients.

sections.heading: What It’s Used For
sections.text: Donepezil is a cognitive enhancer for dementia, used to support memory and daily function rather than to cure the underlying disease.
items: {link:condition:alzheimers-disease:Alzheimer’s Disease}: Approved for mild, moderate, and severe dementia. May improve or stabilize cognition, behavior, and activities of daily living.
Functional support: Extends the time patients can manage self-care tasks like dressing, managing finances, or medication adherence.
Behavioral symptoms: Can modestly help with apathy, attention, and fluctuations in alertness in some patients.
{link:condition:parkinsons-disease-dementia:Parkinson Disease Dementia} (off-label): Used to improve cognition and sometimes visual hallucinations.
{link:condition:dementia-with-lewy-bodies:Dementia with Lewy Bodies} (off-label): Often used when hallucinations, fluctuations, and visuospatial deficits are prominent.
{link:condition:vascular-dementia:Vascular and mixed dementias} (off-label): Occasionally used when Alzheimer’s and vascular contributions overlap.
off_label: Comorbid vascular dementia or “mixed” Alzheimer/vascular presentations

sections.heading: What People and Families Notice

quotes: She seemed more present at the dinner table and followed conversations better.
He started remembering recent events a bit more, like what we had for breakfast.
Day-to-day tasks felt smoother, even if the disease was still there.
We didn’t see much of a change, but we felt better knowing we had tried it.
Things kept slowly getting worse, and we weren’t sure the pill was doing anything.
items.note: Not everyone improves. Sometimes the best outcome is a slower rate of decline that’s hard to see in daily life.

quotes: He had nausea and diarrhea for the first couple of weeks.
Her appetite dropped, and she lost a few pounds.
There were some restless nights and vivid dreams after starting it.
items.note: GI upset and weight loss are common, especially with dose increases. Insomnia and abnormal dreams can also occur.

sections.intro: Experiences with donepezil range from clearly helpful to neutral or occasionally negative. Caregiver observations are critical.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Donepezil’s pharmacologic effect begins quickly, but clinical benefits should be judged over months, not days.
key_points: Steady state: Reached in about 2–3 weeks for oral tablets and roughly 4–6 weeks for the patch.
First month: Common time window for nausea, diarrhea, or insomnia during dose initiation or increase.
6–12 weeks: Typical timeframe to assess whether there is meaningful cognitive or functional benefit.
Long-term: Benefits often plateau; over time, many patients continue to decline, but may do so more slowly vs. without treatment.

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Across trials in mild to severe Alzheimer’s disease, donepezil produces modest average improvements or slower decline on cognitive and functional scales compared with placebo. Some individuals and families notice clear functional gains, while others see little difference. Benefits may be most apparent in attention, orientation, and ability to perform basic and instrumental activities of daily living.
sections.clinical_details: Donepezil is considered a standard first-line cholinesterase inhibitor for Alzheimer’s dementia. Higher doses (eg, 23 mg) may offer small additional cognitive gains over 10 mg for some patients with moderate–severe disease, but at the cost of more GI side effects and weight loss. Treatment decisions should be individualized and revisited periodically as disease progresses.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Donepezil can slow the heart, provoke arrhythmias, and cause significant weight loss or syncope in vulnerable patients.

Rhabdomyolysis: Rare cases of muscle breakdown with elevated CK, muscle pain, dark urine, and kidney injury have been reported.
Peptic ulcer and GI bleeding: Increased gastric acid secretion may worsen ulcers or trigger GI bleeding, especially with NSAIDs or anticoagulants.
Respiratory disease: Can increase bronchoconstriction; use caution in asthma or COPD.
Seizure risk: Cholinergic stimulation may lower seizure threshold in susceptible patients, although seizures can also be due to underlying dementia.
Urinary obstruction: Can increase bladder outflow resistance and worsen symptoms in patients with urinary tract obstruction.

patient_counseling: Report fainting, near-fainting, new palpitations, or falls right away—these may signal slow heart rate or arrhythmia.
Tell your clinician about black stools, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, or severe stomach pain—these may indicate GI bleeding.
Monitor weight regularly. Let your clinician know if you lose more than a few pounds unintentionally.
For the patch: rotate sites each week and remove the old patch before applying a new one. Stop and call your clinician if severe redness, blistering, or itching occurs at the patch site.
Do not stop donepezil suddenly without discussing it. Some patients worsen abruptly when cholinesterase inhibitors are discontinued.

sections.intro: Donepezil is metabolized by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 and enhances cholinergic tone. Both PK and PD interactions matter.

sections.heading: Stopping Donepezil Safely
sections.text: Donepezil is not physically addictive, but abrupt discontinuation can lead to noticeable cognitive or behavioral worsening in some patients.
key_points: Avoid abrupt stop: Unless there is a serious adverse reaction (eg, profound bradycardia, severe GI bleed, or suspected rhabdomyolysis), taper rather than stopping suddenly.
Typical taper: Reduce the dose by ~50% (eg, 10 mg to 5 mg) for about 4 weeks, then stop if tolerated. For very frail patients, a slower taper can be considered.
Patch taper: Step down to a lower-strength patch (if available) or extend the dosing interval before discontinuation, in coordination with the prescriber.
Monitor during taper: Watch for acute worsening in cognition, function, psychosis, or agitation. If clear deterioration occurs, consider resuming the prior dose if appropriate.
End-of-life care: In late-stage dementia or palliative focus, discontinuation is often reasonable; discuss goals of care with family and the interdisciplinary team.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Adults)
sections.text: Dosing is typically once daily for oral formulations and once weekly for the patch, with slow titration to minimize GI and cardiac side effects.

adult.alzheimers_mild_moderate_oral_initial: 5 mg orally once daily, usually at bedtime.
adult.alzheimers_mild_moderate_oral_titration: If tolerated, increase to 10 mg once daily after 4–6 weeks.
adult.alzheimers_moderate_severe_oral: Start at 5 mg once daily; increase to 10 mg once daily after 4–6 weeks. For some patients stable on 10 mg for ≥3 months, a 23 mg once-daily tablet may be considered, though GI side effects increase substantially.
adult.alzheimers_transdermal_initial: Patch delivering 5 mg per 24 hours, applied once weekly.
adult.alzheimers_transdermal_titration: After 4–6 weeks, may increase to 10 mg per 24-hour patch once weekly if tolerated (maximum: 10 mg per 24 hours).
adult.other_dementias_off_label: Parkinson disease dementia, Lewy body dementia, and vascular/mixed dementias are typically dosed like Alzheimer’s: 5 mg once daily, then 10 mg once daily after 4–6 weeks as tolerated.
adult.renal_impairment: Mild to severe kidney impairment, including hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis: generally no dose adjustment required.
adult.elderly_special: Most patients are older adults. Frail patients or those ≥85 years with low body weight may benefit from remaining at 5 mg once daily if higher doses are not clearly helpful or cause side effects.

sections.simple_explanation: Most people start donepezil at 5 mg once a day and, if tolerated, increase to 10 mg a day after a month or so. The patch offers a once-weekly alternative. Higher doses can bring more side effects, so the goal is the lowest dose that seems helpful and well tolerated.

sections.heading: Special Populations
sections.text: Donepezil is used almost exclusively in older adults, often with multiple comorbidities and medications.
sections.pregnancy: Donepezil is rarely used in pregnancy, since dementia syndromes are uncommon in reproductive-age individuals. Animal data show some adverse fetal effects, but human data are limited. If a pregnant patient on donepezil requires ongoing treatment, the potential benefits should clearly outweigh risks, and non-pharmacologic support for cognition should be optimized.
sections.lactation: It is unknown whether donepezil passes into human breast milk. Use in breastfeeding is rarely relevant clinically given the typical age of patients. If needed, risks to the infant, potential benefits to the parent, and alternative treatments should be considered.
sections.pediatrics: Donepezil is not a standard treatment for children or adolescents; pediatric use would be highly specialized and off-label (eg, rare neurodegenerative conditions) and requires subspecialty oversight.

Frailty, low body weight, conduction disease, and polypharmacy (especially cardioactive and QT-prolonging drugs) raise risk. Start low, titrate slowly, and reassess benefit vs. burden regularly.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Donepezil is available as oral tablets, orally disintegrating tablets (ODT), and a once-weekly transdermal patch.
items: Oral tablets: 5 mg, 10 mg, and 23 mg strengths; 23 mg tablet has unique pharmacokinetics and must be swallowed whole.
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT): 5 mg and 10 mg; dissolve on the tongue and are useful for patients with swallowing difficulty.
Transdermal patch (Adlarity): Delivers 5 mg/day or 10 mg/day over 7 days; applied once weekly to the back, upper buttocks, or upper outer thigh.
Multiple generic tablets and ODT formulations: Similar strengths to brand, but excipients may differ.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Alzheimer’s disease involves a deficit of acetylcholine in the cortex and basal forebrain. Donepezil reversibly and noncompetitively inhibits centrally active acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in synapses. By slowing acetylcholine breakdown, donepezil increases its availability for signaling between neurons, which can modestly improve or stabilize cognition and daily functioning in some patients.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Donepezil is a first-line cholinesterase inhibitor for mild, moderate, and severe Alzheimer’s dementia. It is often started early in the course of cognitive decline and continued as long as there is a perceived benefit and side effects remain manageable. In Parkinson disease dementia and Lewy body dementia, it is one of several off-label options used to support cognition and manage hallucinations. Decisions to start, continue, or stop donepezil should be individualized, revisiting goals of care, quality of life, and caregiver input over time—especially in advanced disease and at the end of life.

faqs.a: Donepezil is a memory and thinking medication for people with Alzheimer’s disease, from mild through severe stages. It’s also used off-label in some other dementias, like Parkinson disease dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies, to help with cognition and sometimes hallucinations.

faqs.q: Does donepezil slow down Alzheimer’s disease?
faqs.a: Donepezil does not stop or reverse the underlying disease, but it can slow the rate of decline or improve day-to-day function in some people. The average benefit is modest, but individual responses vary—from clear improvement to no obvious change.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see if donepezil is working?
faqs.a: We usually judge benefit over 2–3 months. Some patients seem more alert or engaged within a few weeks, but a meaningful assessment often requires 8–12 weeks of stable dosing, along with caregiver input about daily functioning.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of donepezil?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are nausea, diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, insomnia or vivid dreams, dizziness, and muscle cramps. These are usually worse when starting or increasing the dose and may improve over time.

faqs.q: Can donepezil cause heart problems or fainting?
faqs.a: Yes. Donepezil can slow the heart rate and sometimes cause heart block, which may lead to dizziness or fainting. This is more concerning in people with existing conduction disease or on medications that also slow the heart. Any episodes of fainting or near-fainting should be reported promptly.

faqs.q: Should donepezil be taken in the morning or at night?
faqs.a: Traditionally it’s given at bedtime, but if it causes insomnia or nightmares, switching to an earlier evening dose or morning dosing can sometimes help. The time of day is less important than consistency and tolerability.

faqs.q: When should we think about stopping donepezil?
faqs.a: Consider tapering if side effects are significant (eg, weight loss, syncope, severe GI symptoms), if there is no perceived benefit after an adequate trial, or in late-stage dementia when the focus shifts to comfort. Stopping should usually be gradual and done in partnership with the care team, with close monitoring for any sudden decline.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between pills and the patch?
faqs.a: Oral donepezil is taken once daily as a tablet or orally disintegrating tablet. The Adlarity patch delivers donepezil continuously through the skin and is changed once weekly. The patch can be helpful for people with swallowing problems or adherence issues, but it can cause skin irritation at the application site.

faqs.q: Can donepezil be used with memantine?
faqs.a: Yes. Donepezil is often combined with memantine in moderate to severe Alzheimer’s disease. They work through different mechanisms and can have additive benefits for some patients, though the overall effect is still modest.

faqs.q: Will stopping donepezil suddenly make dementia much worse?
faqs.a: Some people show a noticeable decline in cognition or behavior after abrupt discontinuation. That’s why we generally taper the dose and monitor closely. If clear worsening occurs after stopping, it may be reasonable to restart in selected cases, depending on overall goals of care and prior tolerability.
